title: AI amplifies what you should have cut, not time itself
dek: Without first defining and cutting what shouldn't be done, AI is merely an accelerator: it creates no free time, only amplifies trivia and distraction into more work.
why: No new theory, but Ferriss squares the Four-Hour Workweek methodology against AI for the first time, offering clear, counterintuitive judgment rather than platitudes.
who: Anyone concerned with how AI reshapes personal productivity, entrepreneurs wondering what to prioritize, and readers revisiting self-help classics but questioning whether they've aged.
skip: Sponsor segments (kitchenware, creatine, AG1, Incogni) can be skipped.

points.h: AI amplifies what you should have cut, not time itself
points.body: The DEAL framework's ‘Define’ and ‘Eliminate’ steps become *more* critical in the AI era, not less. AI is an accelerator—it makes everything you hand it faster. If you haven't already filtered ruthlessly for what truly matters, AI amplifies trivia and distraction into *more* work. Ferriss observes that over nine-tenths of real cases show people using AI to do faster what they shouldn't do at all, creating more work instead of less.

points.h: Set your daily action target smaller than feels achievable
points.body: When facing loss of agency and analysis paralysis, Ferriss's answer is counterintuitive: shrink daily action quota below what you think you can do. Five push-ups. Ten minutes of meditation before sleep. A thank-you call to one person. The point is not immediate large change. It is rebuilding self-identity through small daily wins you *can* keep—‘I am a person who acts’—then gradually scaling up.

points.h: Compress decade goals to six months to break thinking patterns
points.body: Borrowing Peter Thiel's approach, compress a ten-year goal into six months as a thought experiment—not to produce actual answers but to shake loose from habit and force non-obvious paths. Pair this with advance clarity on which six-month milestones unlock more energy. Also red-team yourself: ask friends directly, if this goal or relationship failed completely in two years, what would be the single most likely cause? Force them past polite answers.

points.h: Train the brain to see through blur, don't change lenses
points.body: He recommends Oryx (he's also an investor), software that trains visual processing rather than altering the lens. The brain gets better at reconstructing clear images from blur. His own result: 30 days at 8 minutes daily shifted him from barely reading near text to reading small menus in dim restaurant light. He emphasizes this is not mainstream-validated and remains in early-stage trials.

points.h: Concentrate spending on two things, not cutting across many
points.body: When asked what he's stopped optimizing, he flipped the question (borrowing Ramit Sethi): what if instead he spent ten times more on the one or two things that truly matter? He chose health and relationships. Once you flood those two with ten-fold attention, other ‘productive-looking but time-wasting’ work naturally vanishes for lack of space.

points.h: Answer quality depends on physiology before it depends on technique
points.body: He splits answering into state-story-strategy. Most people skip to strategy, but poor state turns the story into ‘I can't’ or ‘I never will,’ making strategy useless. Before recording, he tunes physiology 15 minutes ahead—exogenous ketones, small doses of caffeine via toothpick, blood-sugar stability—so story shifts. He also notes that silence or ‘that's a good question, let me think’ itself buys the brain processing time.

points.h: Back pain is not reducible to psychological causes
points.body: On John Sarno's book, he concedes friends recovered using it but rejects the thesis that nearly all back pain is psychosomatic. He tests the idea: if someone hit your L5 vertebra with a pry bar, wouldn't it hurt? Wouldn't it leave chronic pain? The answer forces admission. He sees back pain as a blind-person-and-elephant problem—physical therapy, surgery, acupuncture, psychology each touch part of the truth, but no single framework covers everyone.

points.h: Slow carbs and intermittent fasting together work better after forty
points.body: Most Four-Hour Body content holds fifteen years later. His current default stacks slow carbs with intermittent fasting: at least 16 hours fasting, 8-hour eating window, usually starting noon or 1 PM, ending at dinner. One detail: timer starts from the last bite, not the first. He reports four to six weeks shows measurable shifts in oral glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity.

terms.def: Define, Eliminate, Automate, Liberate—the four-step system from The Four-Hour Workweek
Visual-training software that improves presbyopia by training the brain's visual processing, not by lens correction
Asking others to actively find weaknesses and vulnerabilities from an adversarial angle
Compressed-cycle transcranial magnetic stimulation, typically used for depression and anxiety
Modulating autonomic tone by stimulating the vagus nerve
Strength training built on bodyweight and gymnastics movements

facts.v: compressed from 3–4 months to 1 week, then to 1 day with medication
At least 16 hours fasting, 8-hour eating window

quotes.text: AI and so on simply multiplies the useless. It multiplies the unimportant, the trivial, the distracting.
I would do less than you think you're capable of doing. So that you are able to do it daily.
if this company, if this relationship fails in two years, what do you think the most likely reasons would be?
I went from not being able to really read anything at this distance to being able to read a menu with tiny font at night in a restaurant with very dim lighting. And that is fucking bananas.
what would it look like to invest 10 times more in one or two areas that matter most?
if I took a ball-peen hammer to your L5 and just whacked on it like I was trying to chop wood, would that cause pain? Would it cause long-lasting pain?
the best diet that you follow is a lot better than the perfect diet that you quit.
